The hidden challenge of Generative AI is that the model itself is often the simplest part to handle.

Anyone can integrate an LLM API in a single afternoon and create a polished prototype. However, when attempting to scale that demo for real enterprise users, issues like latency spikes and skyrocketing costs can arise, leading to system failures without robust infrastructure.

Interestingly, I learned how to address these challenges before I ever worked with an LLM.

My initial experience in cloud development involved tasks like mapping contact flows, writing serverless Lambdas, and debugging in CloudWatch dashboards. This foundational work taught me how enterprise systems function.

Over the past 4.5 years, I transitioned from managing cloud infrastructure to developing GenAI systems that operate on it. Tools like AWS Bedrock, LangChain, LangGraph, and vector databases became essential in my daily work - not just for creating impressive demos, but for delivering production-grade AI that positively impacts business metrics.

I focus on the outcomes when real users interact with the system, rather than proof-of-concepts that merely exist in presentations. For instance, when tasked with creating an enterprise RAG platform, we engineered a solution that reduced query-resolution latency by 98%, transforming it from minutes to sub-seconds. Also implemented token-level streaming with FastAPI for a seamless experience and automated the source-to-vector ingestion pipeline to eliminate manual efforts.

This is the type of GenAI work I am passionate about: identifying friction points, automating repetitive tasks, and building an LLM layer that operates effectively at scale. Whether it’s creating an automated complaint-letter engine that reduces manual drafting by 95% or integrating an LLM-as-a-judge layer for audit readiness, my focus is on production.

Due to my extensive experience in this field, I have begun teaching. In the past year, I have trained and up-skilled over 21,000 students and working professionals in applied ML and Generative AI. Teaching complex orchestration frameworks to engineers has deepened my understanding of my own technology stack.

Now, I am seeking my next challenge.

I am open to new opportunities and looking for a full-time role as a Generative AI Engineer or Machine Learning Engineer, where I can develop, scale, and deliver impactful AI systems.

text:
Two years ago, "knowing AI" meant you could call an API and write a decent prompt. That bar is gone.

The engineers getting hired and trusted with production systems in 2026 are not the ones who know the most models. They are the ones who understand the system around the model.

After 6+ years shipping these systems, here is the mental map I would hand anyone starting today. 17 concepts, 5 layers.
1- The retrieval layer (1 to 3)
Embedding models, vector databases, RAG. Still, the foundation of almost everything. Most "AI features" in production are retrieval problems wearing an LLM costume.

2- The efficiency layer (4 to 7)
Context engineering, semantic caching, model routing, and AI gateways. This is where the cost and latency battles are won. Nobody notices this layer until the invoice arrives.

3- The action layer (8 to 11)
Function calling, tool use, MCP, and external integrations. The difference between a chatbot that describes work and a system that does it. MCP has quietly become the standard wiring here.

4- The agent layer (12 to 14)
Agent harness, execution loops, memory systems. Where most teams are right now, and where most of the hard, unsolved problems live.

5- The trust layer (15 to 17)
Guardrails, observability, evaluations. The least glamorous layer and the one that decides whether your system survives contact with real users.
The uncomfortable truth: most engineers are strong in one or two layers and hand-wave the rest. The retrieval people ignore evals. The agent people ignore the cost. The infra people ignore what the model outputs. The rare skill in 2026 is knowing how all 17 connect and where your system will break first.

That last part is the actual job. Every broken AI system that lands on my desk fails at a layer boundary: a solid RAG pipeline with no evals, a capable agent with no cost controls. When you carry the full map, diagnosis is fast. That is why we can usually tell a client where their system is bleeding within the first call, before writing a single line of code.

I am Muhammad Ghulam Jillani, Founder and Lead AI Engineer at Jillani SofTech, Top Rated Plus on Upwork. We have delivered 22+ production AI systems across healthcare, finance, legal, and SaaS: agentic RAG platforms, autonomous agents, LLM products, and traditional ML, where it beats GenAI. Real numbers: 91% factual accuracy on a clinical decision support system, 8,000+ daily queries on an enterprise knowledge assistant, 900+ daily workflow triggers on a revenue automation.

Save this as your checklist. Audit your system against all 17 before your users do it for you.

text:
🚀 AI Knowledge Series #2 | RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Which One Should You Choose?
One of the most common questions in the GenAI world is:
"Should I use RAG or Fine-Tuning for my AI application?"
The answer depends on the problem you're solving.
📚 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Think of RAG as giving your LLM access to an up-to-date knowledge library.
✅ No model retraining required
 ✅ Retrieves relevant information from enterprise documents in real time
 ✅ Lower implementation cost and faster deployment
 ✅ Easy to keep knowledge current
 ✅ Best for internal chatbots, document search, customer support, and knowledge assistants
🧠 Fine-Tuning
Fine-tuning teaches a model new behaviors by training it on domain-specific data.
✅ Improves performance for specialized tasks
 ✅ Adapts the model to your business language and workflows
 ✅ Better for structured outputs and domain-specific reasoning
 ⚠️ Requires training data, compute resources, and ongoing maintenance
Ideal for:
Medical AI
Legal AI
Code generation
Financial risk analysis
Highly specialized enterprise applications
💡 When should you choose each?
Choose RAG if:
Your information changes frequently.
You want quick implementation.
You need your AI to reference company documents.
You want lower infrastructure costs.
Choose Fine-Tuning if:
You need the model to learn a new behavior.
Your outputs require a consistent style or format.
You're solving a highly specialized domain problem.
Accuracy depends on adapting the model itself.
🔥 Pro Tip
The most successful enterprise AI solutions today combine RAG + Fine-Tuning:
Fine-Tuning for domain expertise and behavior.
RAG for real-time, up-to-date enterprise knowledge.
This hybrid approach is increasingly becoming the standard for production-grade GenAI systems.
